title: A Game of Pai Sho
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 6 of 40
content:
Iroh taught me pai sho by letting me lose.

“You are not even pretending to be kind,” I said after my third defeat.

He gathered the tiles with a satisfied hum. “Kindness and strategy are not opposites.”

“You moved three pieces I didn’t know existed.”

“That is because you did not ask what they did.”

“I assumed they were decorative.”

“A common mistake.”

The tea shop was closed for the afternoon. Iroh had set up the game board on a low table near the window. Sunlight lay across the painted tiles. Outside, Ba Sing Se moved through its ordinary noise: carts, voices, distant bells.

Inside, the world had narrowed to red and white pieces, jasmine tea, and Iroh's hand resting beside mine.

“What is the object of the game?” I asked.

“To create harmony.”

“You could have told me that before you destroyed me.”

“Then you might have tried to create harmony too early.”

“Is that bad?”

“Harmony is not the same as peace. Sometimes the board must become complicated before it can become balanced.”

I studied the pieces. “That sounds like something you say when you are winning.”

“It is something I say because I am winning.”

I threw a tile at him. It struck his shoulder and bounced into my lap.

Iroh laughed so loudly that a customer outside the shop turned to look through the window.

“You are a dangerous player,” he said.

“I’m an unconventional player.”

“You are holding a flower tile upside down.”

“Unconventional.”

He reached across the board and turned it for me. His fingers brushed mine.

Iroh slid one tile aside and turned the board so I could see the empty spaces he had been protecting.

"Wait," I said. "You let me take the center."

"I did."

"On purpose?"

"You were so pleased with yourself that I thought it would be cruel to interrupt."

I stared at him. "You gave me a victory so you could take three others."

"A useful description of a very poor bargain."

I moved my hand toward the red dragon, then stopped. His expression changed just enough to tell me he had noticed. I chose a smaller tile instead.

"Is that the clever move?" I asked.

"That depends. What do you want from it?"

"To keep the pieces I like."

"Then you have finally begun to play your own game."

Outside, a cartwheel struck a loose stone. Iroh glanced toward the window before looking back at the board. There was a military precision to the way he counted possible moves; it sat beside his ridiculous delight in watching me discover a trap. I liked both parts of him. I was also beginning to recognize how dangerous it would be to confuse the second with innocence.

"You could have told me that ten minutes ago," I said.

"Would you have listened?"

"Absolutely not."

His laughter warmed the little room. I leaned forward to take a different tile, and he waited with one hand open beside the board. I didn't know whether he meant it as an invitation or simply a place to rest his hand. When our fingers touched, neither of us hurried to explain it.

The contact was brief, but it changed the room.

Iroh looked at my hand, then at my face. “You are distracted.”

“You are sitting very close.”

“The board is small.”

“The table is large.”

“An excellent observation.”

I moved my hand away. He did not chase it.

“Are you regretting last night?” I asked.

Iroh's expression softened. “No.”

“You answer quickly.”

“Some questions deserve a quick answer.”

“And some?”

“Some deserve tea first.”

He poured. I watched the steam rise between us.

“Do you regret it?” he asked.

“No.”

“Then we are in agreement.”

“That was not the question I asked.”

“You are right.”

The honesty warmed me more than the tea.

“I’m not used to this,” I said.

“To losing at pai sho?”

“To someone being careful with me and still wanting me.”

Iroh's fingers tightened around his cup.

“People often confuse desire with permission,” he said. “They believe wanting someone gives them the right to hurry.”

“You don’t hurry.”

“I have hurried before.”

“You?”

“I was young.”

“You’re making yourself sound ancient.”

“I am ancient compared to the tea leaves.”

“That is not how age works.”

“It is how tea works.”

I smiled, but the question remained.

“Why are you not hurrying now?” I asked.

Iroh set his cup down. “Because I would rather be certain you are walking toward me than discover you were only trying to keep up.”

The words went through me.

“You make it very difficult to be casual.”

“I have been accused of that.”

“By whom?”

“My nephew. He believes my habit of offering wisdom at breakfast is a form of attack.”

“He may be right.”

“He is often right. It is one of his more irritating qualities.”

The shop door opened. A messenger entered to deliver a bundle of tea. Iroh stood to sign for it. I watched the way he moved, broad and graceful, carrying a lifetime of discipline without letting it harden him.

When he returned, he placed a small white tile beside my hand.

“What does that do?” I asked.

“It waits.”

“That is a terrible game piece.”

“Only if you believe waiting means doing nothing.”

“You are going to say that patience is a strategy.”

“Patience is a strategy.”

I sighed. “I should have guessed.”

He taught me the names of the pieces. The white lotus. The red dragon. The wheel. The knot of destiny. Each tile carried a meaning, but none were absolute. A piece could support, obstruct, or transform depending on what surrounded it.

“That sounds like people,” I said.

“People are more complicated. They cannot be placed neatly on a board.”

“You would be surprised what people try to do with me.”

Iroh looked at me. “I would not be surprised.”

The comment was so quiet I nearly missed it.

“What do you mean?”

“You have the posture of someone who has been assigned roles without being asked.”

I looked down at the board.

“The fixer,” I said. “The easy one. The person who leaves before being left.”

“And who are you when nobody is assigning you a role?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then we will not decide today.”

He moved the white lotus.

Before I could take my turn, a boy appeared at the doorway holding a broken wooden tile. He couldn't have been much older than twelve. The grain had split straight through a wheel.

“My grandfather says you can tell where a board was made by the flower on the back,” he told Iroh. “Is that true?”

Iroh held out his hand, and the boy gave him the piece. He turned it over. Someone had scratched a crooked blossom into the wood.

“It can tell you who made this tile,” he said. “Not necessarily where they learned to play.”

“Grandfather says it came from a White Lotus master.”

“Your grandfather may be right.” Iroh placed the halves together. “Would he mind if I asked him rather than guessing?”

I watched the boy's disappointment settle into curiosity.

“You don't know?”

“I know more now than when you arrived,” Iroh said. “For example, I know the wood has split where someone tried to repair it with a nail. That is useful. And I know that the person who remembers its history is not standing in this room.”

Mina found a small cloth and wrapped the halves. She wrote the grandfather's address on a slip, correcting the boy when he left out the alley number. Iroh didn't announce he would restore the tile. He asked whether they wanted help finding a carpenter.

Once the boy left, I pointed at the lotus on our board.

“Were you going to use that as a lesson about patience?”

“I was considering it.”

“That's unbearable.”

“Then I am fortunate you haven't learned to defeat me yet.”

He pushed the tile toward me. It was my move, and for once he wasn't pretending my choice could be made for me.

“Your turn.”

I studied the board. The last game had been lost because I tried to protect one piece. This time, I let it go. I moved the wheel, then placed the lotus near the center.

Iroh's brows lifted.

“Was that good?” I asked.

“It was interesting.”

“You say that when you don’t want to admit I’m winning.”

“You are not winning.”

“Yet.”

“A dangerous word.”

The game lasted until the sun lowered. I did not win, but I forced Iroh to think. When he finally placed his last piece, he looked pleased rather than triumphant.

“You have improved,” he said.

“You sound surprised.”

“I am delighted.”

He gathered the tiles. My hands met over the red dragon.

Neither of us moved.

“Can I kiss you again?” I asked.

Iroh's smile was slow. “You may.”

The kiss began across the board. It was awkward because the table was between us, and Iroh laughed when I nearly knocked over the tea. I moved around the table. He rose to meet me.

His hands settled at my shoulders. When I stepped closer, they moved to my waist. The warmth of him gathered beneath my palms.

“Still comfortable?” he murmured.

“Yes.”

“Still certain?”

“Ask me tomorrow.”

He kissed me more deeply. His beard brushed my skin, soft and surprising. I smiled against his mouth.

“What?” he asked.

“You taste like jasmine.”

“A professional hazard.”

“A pleasant one.”

The shop's closing bell sounded even though the door was locked. Iroh pulled back with a sigh.

“The kettle,” he said.

“Your other lover?”

“It is demanding.”

He went to check it, and I followed. The kiss remained between us, not finished, only paused.

That night, when I climbed the stairs to my room, a single white lotus tile rested on the windowsill.

Beside it was a note in Iroh's careful handwriting: WAITING IS NOT DOING NOTHING.

I smiled until I fell asleep.

I woke before sunrise with the white lotus tile still in my hand.

For a moment, I did not remember where I was. Then the room returned: the slanted ceiling, the jasmine plant, the faint warmth rising through the floor from the kitchen below.

The note lay on the windowsill. I read it again.

WAITING IS NOT DOING NOTHING.

I carried the tile downstairs.

Iroh was already awake, standing over a kettle with an expression of deep suspicion.

“It whistled at me,” he said.

“Perhaps it wants breakfast.”

“It wants authority.”

I placed the tile on the counter. “You left this.”

“I did.”

“Why?”

“Because you were trying to win by protecting every piece.”

“That sounds like a criticism.”

“It is an observation.”

“You are very fond of observations.”

“They are safer than predictions.”

I looked at the tile. “What were you predicting?”

Iroh's hand went still on the kettle handle.

“That you might decide last night was a mistake,” he said.

The honesty was quiet, without the armor of humor.

“I didn’t,” I replied.

“I am pleased.”

“You could have asked.”

“I could have.”

“You are learning too.”

“Every day.”

I moved around the counter. He waited for me to close the distance.

“The game is not the only place where I protect every piece,” I said.

“No.”

“I want to stop.”

“You may begin with one.”

I touched his hand. “This one.”

Iroh's eyes warmed.

He kissed me in the quiet kitchen while the kettle simmered. There was no board between us this time. His arms held me close, but his body remained attentive to every change in mine.

When the shop opened, I placed the white lotus tile beside the register.

“Are you keeping it there?” he asked.

“It is watching the game.”

“It has a very important position.”

“It is waiting.”

Iroh smiled. “Not doing nothing.”

The day began.

I kept the white lotus tile near the register. Every time someone asked about it, Iroh answered that it was waiting for the right move.

I never corrected him.

The next game lasted longer. I still lost, but Iroh had to think before claiming the final space.

He looked delighted.

“You are enjoying my defeat,” I said.

“I am enjoying your persistence.”

“That is a nicer answer.”

“It is also true.”

I smiled.

The game waited.

Patiently.

As I learned.
